paras: The lynching of Walter Davis took place on the night of October 1, 1903, in Marshall, Texas, when a mob of several hundred men broke into the city jail, took Davis, a Black prisoner, and hanged him to a tree. Davis had been arrested hours earlier, after a constable named Hayes was shot from ambush. The story ran across the country through a single wire dispatch, much of which stressed that the militia sent to guard the jail arrived too late.

On the morning of October 1, Constable Hayes was shot from ambush while taking a Black man to jail, and the dispatch said he was "literally riddled with bullets." Shortly afterward Walter Davis and two other Black men were arrested and lodged in the Marshall jail. The dispatch did not say what evidence tied any of the three to the shooting.

A mob formed during the afternoon and attacked the jail. That night several hundred men forced their way through its brick wall using a telephone pole, sledge hammers and crowbars, took out Davis, and marched him to the west side of town, where he was hanged. The Dallas News correspondent and the Paducah Sun said he was hanged to a willow tree.

The Marshall Musketeers, a local militia company, were ordered out but reached the jail after the mob had secured Davis. According to the Associated Press variant, part of the mob talked with the militia officers while others "slipped the negro out and spirited him away." The Paducah Sun's version added that just before the hanging Davis said he had not meant to kill Hayes when he shot, and that when told he would be hanged he said, "I don't want to die that way." In that account he was told to pray, was strung up in a hurry when someone said the militia was coming, and several shots were fired at his body.

The dispatch closed with "Everything is now quiet." No report of an inquest, arrests of mob members, or grand jury action appears in the coverage, and the fate of the two other men arrested with Davis is not reported.

Nearly every report reproduced one Marshall dispatch, which appeared as a Dallas News special and under Associated Press credit in papers from Richmond to Honolulu on October 2. Two forms circulated: one describing the telephone pole and the Musketeers, and a shorter one in which the mob "battered its way into the jail" and part of it talked with the militia. Weeklies and news digests carried one-line versions into late October, such as the Cooperstown Courier's "A mob lynched Walter Davis (colored) at Marshall, Tex., for the murder of Constable Hayes."

Although the dispatch said only that the lynching was "the result of" the constable's killing, many white headlines treated Davis's guilt as settled. The Bisbee Daily Review called him the "Officer's Slayer," the Paducah Sun said he "Assisted in Murder," and the Arizona Republican headed the story "A Swift Punishment" with "Murder in the Morning Avenged by a Mob Last Night." On October 21 the Anderson Intelligencer stated flatly that Davis had shot "Marshal Hayes" from ambush. The Minneapolis Journal took a different tone, heading the item "This Mob Succeeded" and "Lynching In Texas-Victim a Negro, of Course."

The only Black-press report found was in the Baltimore Afro-American on October 10, which ran the Associated Press variant as a "Special" under the head "Militia Came Too Late. Mob Got Their Quarry Out and Quietly Lynched Him." Its text matched the white papers' wire copy and added no comment, so the Black press as found offered no separate account of Davis or of the constable's killing.

Reports differed on what Davis was accused of: the dispatch named no charge, the Paducah Sun said he assisted in the murder, and the Newport Weekly Independent said he was "charged with murdering an officer." The officer's name appeared as Hayes in most papers and as Hays in the Butte Inter Mountain and the Tupelo Journal, and the Tupelo Journal's headline gave the mob as "Two Hundred Men" while its text said several hundred.

Davis was hanged by a mob of 'several hundred men' who forced the jail with no lawful authority (A1, A9); every report ties the hanging to the ambush killing of Constable Hayes that morning, for which Davis was described as charged (A1, A28).

About twenty white papers and the Baltimore Afro-American printed the story, but every full version repeats the wording of one Marshall dispatch sent out by the Dallas News and the Associated Press (A5, A1, A6, A32); no report contradicts it.

accounts.gist: A mob formed in the afternoon, broke through the jail wall that night, took Davis and hanged him on the west side of town; the militia came too late, and part of the mob talked with its officers while others slipped Davis out.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch under factual heads such as 'Hanged to a Tree' and 'Texas Mob Acts' (A2, A1).
Headlines treated Davis's guilt as settled: 'Officer's Slayer', 'Texas Negro Who Assisted in Murder Lynched', and 'A Swift Punishment / Murder in the Morning Avenged'.
The Minneapolis Journal's head 'This Mob Succeeded / Lynching In Texas-Victim a Negro, of Course' was sardonic about Southern lynching while reprinting the wire text unchanged.
The Baltimore Afro-American printed the AP variant as a 'Special' under 'Militia Came Too Late. Mob Got Their Quarry Out and Quietly Lynched Him,' with no editorial comment.
